t: The stone carries one priestly decree in three scripts, the language of the gods, of documents and of the Greeks, with only minor differences between them.
Its decipherment was the work of many scholars over two decades, from Silvestre de Sacy and Åkerblad on the Demotic to Young and finally Champollion in 1822.
Taken by the British from the French in 1801 and shown in London ever since, it has been the subject of Egyptian requests for its return since 2003.
dyk: The stone's dark colour, which led to its long identification as black basalt, came from a layer of carnauba wax added in London; cleaning in 1999 revealed dark grey granodiorite with a pink vein.
ev: A congress of priests at Memphis issued the decree establishing the divine cult of Ptolemy V
Pierre-François Bouchard spotted the inscribed slab during work on Fort Julien near Rosetta
The stone passed to the British under the Capitulation of Alexandria
It went on display at the British Museum
The first published translations of the Greek text appeared
Jean-François Champollion announced his alphabet of phonetic hieroglyphs in Paris
It left the museum for one month to be shown at the Louvre beside Champollion's Lettre
Zahi Hawass called for the stone to be returned to Egypt

f.made: Inscribed with the Memphis decree, issued by a congress of priests gathered at Memphis on behalf of Ptolemy V Epiphanes of the Ptolemaic dynasty
f.form: A fragment of a larger stele of dark grey granodiorite, 112.3 cm high, 75.7 cm wide and 28.4 cm thick, weighing about 760 kg; 14 surviving lines of hieroglyphs, 32 of Demotic and 54 of Greek
f.where: The British Museum in London (EA 24), on display almost continuously since 1802
f.known: The key to deciphering Egyptian hieroglyphs; Champollion's announcement of 1822; Thomas Young's work on cartouches; its finding at Fort Julien in 1799; its transfer to Britain in 1801; the most visited object in the British Museum; Egyptian calls for its return
